verses.text: Some time later Joseph was told, "Your father is ill." So he set out with his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim.
When Jacob was told, "Your son Joseph has come to you," Israel rallied his strength and sat up in bed.
Jacob said to Joseph, "God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan, and there He blessed me
and told me, 'Behold, I will make you fruitful and multiply you; I will make you a multitude of peoples, and will give this land to your descendants after you as an everlasting possession.'
And now your two sons born to you in Egypt before I came to you here shall be reckoned as mine; Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, just as Reuben and Simeon are mine.
Any children born to you after them shall be yours, and they shall be called by the names of their brothers in the territory they inherit.

Now as for me, when I was returning from Paddan, to my sorrow Rachel died along the way in the land of Canaan, some distance from Ephrath. So I buried her there beside the road to Ephrath" (that is, Bethlehem).
When Israel saw the sons of Joseph, he asked, "Who are these?"
Joseph said to his father, "They are the sons God has given me in this place." So Jacob said, "Please bring them to me, that I may bless them."
Now Israel's eyesight was poor because of old age; he could hardly see. Joseph brought his sons to him, and his father kissed them and embraced them.
"I never expected to see your face again," Israel said to Joseph, "but now God has let me see your children as well."
Then Joseph removed his sons from his father's knees and bowed facedown.
And Joseph took both of them—with Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel's left hand, and Manasseh in his left hand toward Israel's right hand—and brought them close to him.
But Israel stretched out his right hand and put it on the head of Ephraim, the younger; and crossing his hands, he put his left on Manasseh's head, although Manasseh was the firstborn.
Then he blessed Joseph and said: "May the God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has been my shepherd all my life to this day,

the angel who has redeemed me from all harm— may He bless these boys. And may they be called by my name and the names of my fathers Abraham and Isaac, and may they grow into a multitude upon the earth."
When Joseph saw that his father had placed his right hand on Ephraim's head, he was displeased and took his father's hand to move it from Ephraim's head to Manasseh's.
"Not so, my father!" Joseph said. "This one is the firstborn; put your right hand on his head."

But his father refused. "I know, my son, I know!" he said. "He too shall become a people, and he too shall be great; nevertheless, his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his offspring shall become a multitude of nations."
So that day Jacob blessed them and said: "By you shall Israel pronounce this blessing: 'May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh.'" So he put Ephraim before Manasseh.
Then Israel said to Joseph, "Look, I am about to die, but God will be with you and bring you back to the land of your fathers.
And to you, as one who is above your brothers, I give the ridge of land that I took from the Amorites with my sword and bow."

context.author: Genesis names no author. Jewish and Christian tradition, and the New Testament’s way of speaking of “the Law of Moses” (Luke 24:44), credit the five books of the Law to Moses. Many scholars think Genesis was gathered and shaped from older sources over a long time, and a few remarks look back from a later day: “at that time the Canaanites were in the land” (Genesis 12:6).
context.genre: Family narrative: the story of Joseph and his brothers (Genesis 37 to 50)
context.audience: Israel, the twelve tribes, learning how their fathers came down to Egypt and how God turned evil to good
context.setting: Joseph hears that his father is ill and comes with his two sons (v.1). Israel sits up in bed and recalls how “God Almighty appeared to me at Luz” and promised the land (vv.2-4). He adopts Joseph’s sons: “Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, just as Reuben and Simeon are mine” (v.5). He remembers Rachel’s death on the road to Bethlehem (v.7). Almost blind, he kisses the boys: “I never expected to see your face again… but now God has let me see your children as well” (v.11). Joseph places Manasseh, the elder, at his father’s right hand and Ephraim at his left, but Israel crosses his hands and puts his right hand on Ephraim (vv.13-14). He blesses them in the name of “the God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has been my shepherd all my life to this day, the angel who has redeemed me from all harm” (vv.15-16). Joseph tries to move his father’s hand, but Jacob refuses: “I know, my son, I know!… his younger brother shall be greater than he” (vv.17-19). “May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh,” Israel will say in blessing (v.20). Jacob gives Joseph “the ridge of land” he took from the Amorites (v.22).
context.custom: Adopting grandsons as sons was a way of giving Joseph a double share: two tribes instead of one. Joseph receives the rights of the firstborn that Reuben lost (1 Chronicles 5:1-2). The right hand meant the greater blessing. The word for “ridge” in v.22 is shechem, shoulder or slope, likely a play on the city of Shechem, where Joseph would be buried (Joshua 24:32). Jewish parents still bless their sons on Sabbath eve with the words of v.20, “May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh.”
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 49: Jacob gathers all twelve sons and speaks a blessing over each.
context.timelineBible: Once again the younger is put ahead of the elder, as with Abel, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph. Jacob calls God his shepherd for the first time in the Bible (v.15), the picture David later takes up: “The LORD is my shepherd” (Psalm 23:1). Ephraim becomes the leading tribe of the north, so that the prophets can call the whole northern kingdom Ephraim (Hosea 11:8). Hebrews counts this blessing as an act of faith (Hebrews 11:21).

translation.meaning: Usually to act wisely; here perhaps to cross the hands deliberately. Jacob knew what he was doing (v.19).
To pasture, to shepherd. Jacob, a shepherd all his life, calls God the one who shepherded him.
To redeem, to act as a kinsman who buys back. The first use of the word for God’s rescue in the Bible; Boaz is a goel in Ruth.

gospelParallels.note: By faith Jacob blessed each of Joseph’s sons.
The older will serve the younger, by God’s choosing.

overview.summary: Dying Jacob adopts Joseph’s sons Ephraim and Manasseh as his own and blesses them with crossed hands, putting the younger, Ephraim, ahead.

history.t: Ephraim and Manasseh become tribes of Israel.
Later the leading tribe of the northern kingdom.

customs.t: Grandsons counted as sons gave Joseph a double share.
The hand of the greater blessing.

archaeology.t: Show adoption used to pass on inheritance.
The ridge of land given to Joseph, where his bones were buried.

overview.discussion: Jacob, who had schemed for blessing all his life, now gives it freely and calls God the shepherd “all my life to this day” (v.15). Looking back, where can I see that God was shepherding me?
overview.book: The book of Genesis · 50 chapters. Beginnings: creation, the fall, the flood and the nations, then God’s promise to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph.

historicalImage.caption: Jacob Blessing the Sons of Joseph, by Rembrandt (1656, Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister, Kassel). The old man’s right hand rests on the younger boy, Ephraim, while Joseph gently tries to move it (Genesis 48:17-19).

currentImage.caption: Shechem (Nablus) in the pass below Mount Gerizim, in a lantern slide from about 1915. Abram’s first stop in Canaan was “the site of the Oak of Moreh at Shechem,” where he built his first altar (Genesis 12:6-7).
